newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels meet for 2nd round of hostage talks - FEB 14.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels meet for 2nd round of hostage talks - FEB 14.

text.p: The Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 captives at the Japanese ambassador's home on Friday began a second round this week of face-to-face talks to end the 59-day-old siege, the Red Cross said.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo walked into a safe house across the street from the diplomatic compound at about 3:00 p.m (2000 GMT), and minutes later a rebel, believed to be No. 2 leader Rolly Rojas, was ferried over in a Red Cross car.
As the Red Cross car pulled out of the compound, Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebel hymns were heard coming from inside the residence, witnessses said.
The two sides last met on Tuesday, when direct talks between the government and the rebels broke weeks of deadlock in ending the crisis.
Friday's negotiations began amid less security than on Tuesday, when police moved scores of sharpshooters and special forces into the upscale San Isidro district where the residence is located.
Despite the renewed talks, a quick and peaceful solution to the crisis that began when rebels of the MRTA stormed a cocktail party on Dec. 17 was unlikely.
The MRTA has refused to back down on its main demand of freedom for some 400 imprisoned rebels in exchange for the hostages' lives and the government refuses even to discuss the issue.

Also at the talks were members of Peru's guarantors' commission, made up of Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent as well as Japan's observer Teruke Terada.
Tuesday's meeting produced a pledge for further talks but little more apparent progress toward a solution.
The hostages, all men and mostly middle-aged, have spent Christmas, New Year's and now Valentine's Day away from their loved ones.

The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages but have freed most of them. The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian envoys, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro.
